en: The Sutra on the Causes and Conditions of the Thousand Buddhas, translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Kumārajīva of Kucha during the Later Qin dynasty.
Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying on Vulture Peak Mountain in the city of Rājagṛha, together with...
There was a great assembly of five thousand bhikṣus, whose names were:

the Venerable Ājñātakauṇḍinya, the Venerable Uruvilvākāśyapa, the Venerable Gayākāśyapa, the Venerable Nadīkāśyapa, the Venerable Mahākāśyapa, the Venerable Śāriputra, the Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana, the Venerable Kātyāyana, the Venerable Aniruddha, the Venerable Ānanda, and others.

They were all great arhats, renowned among the multitude; like well-trained elephant kings, they had accomplished what was to be done, possessed the three knowledges and the six supernormal powers, and were endowed with the eight liberations.
There were eighty-four thousand bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, headed by the Bodhisattvas Brahmā-Śrī, Viśuddha-caryā, and Ananta-caryā;
and with Bhadrapāla and Ananta acting as co-leaders, there were also the Bodhisattvas Candrasvara from other realms, Candragarbha, and Gadgadasvara as their leaders.

Such great bodhisattvas as these had all long cultivated pure conduct (*brahmacarya*), were peaceful, secure, and pure, and dwelt in the Śūraṅgama Samādhi. They were all fully endowed with the eighty-four thousand pāramitās, manifesting as Buddhas in the Sahā world and in the lands of the ten directions, turning the wondrous wheel of Dharma, and manifesting parinirvāṇa. On Vulture Peak Mountain, at the Ascetic’s Lecture Hall, they all let out the lion’s roar.
These bodhisattva-mahāsattvas each spoke of their own past causes and conditions, and such sounds filled the entire trichiliocosm.
The great assembly—devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, humans, non-humans, and all others—all gathered together.
At that time, the World-Honored One emerged from the stone chamber and asked Ānanda:
"What are all these śrāvakas and bodhisattvas currently discussing?"
Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
Each of the assembly of bodhisattvas has individually recounted the causes and conditions of their past lives.”

At that time, the World-Honored One proceeded slowly and steadily like a great dragon-elephant; having donned his saṃghāṭī robe, he entered the midst of the great assembly and addressed the bodhisattvas, saying:
“What meaning do you each now proclaim?”
That great sound filled the entire world-system.

Bodhisattva Bhadrapāla immediately rose from his seat, prepared a lion throne for the World-Honored One himself, prostrated with his head at the Buddha’s feet, invited the Buddha to take his seat, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
"I wish to inquire briefly today; I only pray that the World-Honored One will explain it for me!
When these words were spoken, eighty-four thousand bodhisattvas each removed their necklaces and scattered them over the Buddha as an offering.
The scattered necklaces remained above the Buddha’s head, as majestic and magnificent as Mount Sumeru, and within mountain caves therein sat a thousand transformation Buddhas.
At that time, the bodhisattvas prostrated at the Buddha’s feet and, with one voice, addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
World-Honored One, what merits did the thousand Buddhas of the Bhadrakalpa plant in past lives,
and what paths and practices did they cultivate,

such that they were always born in the same place and belonged to the same family; and how is it that within a single kalpa, they shall successively attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, transform and deliver all sentient beings in this turbid and evil world, and cause them to firmly resolve upon the three kinds of pure bodhicitta?

For the sake of ourselves and all sentient beings of future ages, we pray that you will extensively analyze and explain the past lives, the various *pāramitās*, the original deeds, and the karmic fruits and retributions of the thousand bodhisattvas of the Bhadrakalpa!
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bodhisattvas, saying:
“Listen attentively, listen attentively!
Reflect upon this well!”
"I shall now analyze and explain this for you in detail. Bhadrapāla!

You should know that in the past, beyond immeasurable, incalculable hundreds of thousands of myriads of koṭis of asaṃkhyeya kalpas, and even more than that number, at that time, this Sahā world was named Great Adornment, and the kalpa was named Great Jewel."

There was a Buddha, a World-Honored One, named Ratnolka-rāja Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidya-caraṇa-saṃpanna, Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttara, Puruṣadamyasārathi, Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām, Buddha, World-Honored One, who appeared in the world.
When that Buddha, the World-Honored One, appeared in the world, he likewise taught and transformed sentient beings through the three vehicles.
The Buddha’s lifespan was half a kalpa; the True Dharma remained in the world for one kalpa, and the Semblance Dharma remained in the world for two kalpas.

During the period of the Semblance Dharma, there was a great king named Guṇaprabha who transformed the people through the ten wholesome paths of action; his realm was peaceful and blissful, like that of a wheel-turning monarch.
At that time, the great king instructed all the people to recite the Vedas.

At that time, there were one thousand youths in the schoolhouse, each fifteen years of age, who were intelligent and possessed great knowledge; they heard the bhikṣus praising the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha.
A youth named Padmaśrī addressed the bhikṣu Kalyāṇakīrti, saying:
"What is meant by 'Buddha'?
What is meant by 'Dharma'?"
"What is meant by 'Saṃgha'?
The bhikṣu answered in verse:
"Those who have fulfilled the pāramitās, Whose pure nature awakens wisdom,"
Having attained accomplishment through supreme mind, he is therefore named Buddha;
with an undefiled nature that is pure, forever transcending the world,
and not observing the five aggregates of the world, his eternal abiding is called Dharma.
"With body and mind always unconditioned, Forever free from the four kinds of nutriment, Serving as a noble field of merit for the world— Therefore they are called the Bhikṣu Saṃgha.

At that time, having heard the names of the Triple Gem, the thousand youths each took incense and flowers and followed the bhikṣu to the monastic quarters. They entered the stūpa to pay homage and beheld the image of the Buddha; the dimensions of that image’s body were sixty-two nayutas of yojanas, and it was fully endowed with eighty-four thousand marks and signs of excellence.
At that time, having seen the Buddha’s image, the thousand youths said to the bhikṣu:
“By what merit did such a superior person, a Great Unsurpassed One, cultivate himself in past lives as to attain such unsurpassed and supreme marks?”
The bhikṣu replied: "Good son! Listen attentively now!"

The World-Honored Buddha, having practiced the eighty-four thousand pāramitās in the past and likewise cultivated the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment, has thus attained such a dignified and majestic body.

The body of the Tathāgata possesses not only these eighty-four thousand gateways of primary and secondary marks, but also the ten powers, the four fearlessnesses, the eighteen unique qualities, great compassion, the three foundations of mindfulness, the three clarities, the six supernormal knowledges, the eight liberations, and so forth.
At that time, having heard the bhikṣu’s praise of the Buddha, the thousand youths prostrated themselves with their five limbs touching the ground and made this great vow before the image:
"We now each resolve to attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi; after incalculable kalpas, we shall surely achieve Buddhahood, equal to and no different from the World-Honored One as he is now."
The third youth, named Padmagarbha, further made this vow:

"Because of this bhikṣu, we have now heard the names of the Triple Gem and have also beheld the physical form of the Tathāgata; thus, there is no doubt that we shall attain Buddhahood in a future age.
Until we achieve Buddhahood, may we always be born in the same place as this bhikṣu."

"Bhadrapāla! You should know now that when those thousand youths heard the names of the Triple Gem, their bodies and minds were filled with joy. At the end of their respective lifespans, they all passed away;
at the moment of death, by the power of the roots of goodness from having heard the Triple Gem, they eliminated the karma of birth and death for fifty-one kalpas."
After the end of his life, he attained rebirth in the Brahma world, which is the natural law for devas.

Having been born in the Brahma palace, he immediately attained three recollections: he remembered that in a past life he had heard the names of the Triple Gem, and by this cause and condition, he was able to be born in the heavens.

At that time, the thousand Brahma kings each mounted a celestial palace and, together with the various Brahmās, held flowers made of the seven precious gems and went before the ancient stupa to make offerings to the Buddha image.
Then the thousand Brahma kings, with one voice and in unison, spoke these verses:
"The Sun of Wisdom of Great Renown, Dwells long in the state of sublime tranquility."
"Hearing his name removes all evils, And one naturally arises in the Brahma-world;
I now prostrate with my head at his feet, Taking refuge in Great Liberation.
Having spoken this verse, they each returned to the Brahma-world.
“Bhadrapāla! You should know now that the king of that time who transformed people through the ten wholesome paths has long since attained Buddhahood—he is Vipaśyin Tathāgata;
the bhikṣu named Kīrtivardhana is Śikhin Tathāgata.”
"Bhadrapāla, were those thousand youths anyone else?
They are none other than the Buddha Krakucchanda of the present age, and so on, up to the final Tathāgata Ruci."

You should now know that I and the thousand bodhisattvas of this Bhadrakalpa heard the names of the Triple Gem from that Buddha and first resolved our minds upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*; such was the manner of its occurrence.
The Buddha told Bhadrapāla:

"You should now know that I recall, in the past, immeasurable, incalculable, and asankhyeya kalpas ago, there was a great kingdom in this Sahā world named Vārāṇasī. Its king was named Brahmadatta, who constantly transformed the people through the wholesome Dharma; at that time, the human lifespan was eighty-four thousand kalpas."

At that time, King Brahmadatta, seeing the signs of his own decline, entrusted the kingdom to his son and went forth to study the Way. He left the household life at dawn in the Udumbara grove, the birthplace of the sages.

Sitting upright in meditation for the duration of a single meal, he contemplated the twelve links of dependent origination in both forward and reverse order; after observing them eighteen times in this manner, he immediately attained the path of a Pratyekabuddha and leaped into the air, performing the eighteen miraculous transformations.
In the Udumbara forest, there were five hundred brahmins who saw upon the soles of the feet of a pratyekabuddha the characters of the twelve links of dependent origination:

ignorance conditions volitional formations; volitional formations condition consciousness; consciousness conditions name-and-form; name-and-form conditions the six sense bases; the six sense bases condition contact; contact conditions feeling; feeling conditions craving; craving conditions clinging; clinging conditions existence; existence conditions birth; and birth conditions old age, death, grief, lamentation, suffering, and despair.

When the five hundred brahmins saw these words, some contemplated how conditioned phenomena arise from ignorance (*avidyā*) without any underlying basis; three hundred of them immediately attained the path of a *pratyekabuddha*.
Furthermore, two hundred people contemplated the links of ignorance, formations, craving, grasping, and existence, and they immediately attained the state of a *pratyekabuddha*.
Others contemplated the sequence from ignorance through old age, death, sorrow, lamentation, suffering, and despair, and by means of the practice of impermanence, they became *pratyekabuddhas*.
Within a single day, five hundred and one pratyekabuddhas appeared in the world in the Udumbara grove.
At that time, the great earth shook in six ways, as did all the celestial palaces up to the Brahma realm.

At that time, each of the thousand Brahma kings took *mandārava* flowers, *mahāmandārava* flowers, *mañjūṣaka* flowers, and *mahāmañjūṣaka* flowers in their robes and went to the Udumbara grove to make offerings to the Pratyekabuddhas. Prostrating at their feet with their heads, they said:
"O Great Virtuous Ones!..."
"Please preach the Dharma for me.
At that time, the Pratyekabuddha leaped into the air and performed the eighteen transformations, extending his hands and revealing his feet.

Then, the thousand Brahmā kings saw the appearance of the characters of the Twelve Links of Dependent Origination beneath his feet; they saw the text of the Ten Wholesome Actions in his palms; and within the light of his crown, they saw the Dharma of the Five Precepts and the text of the Eightfold Uposatha.
At that time, the thousand Brahma kings were filled with joy in body and mind; they received, upheld, read, and recited [the teaching], and made this great vow:

"We have now seen these noble beings sitting cross-legged as if entering meditative concentration, their bodies radiating light, and these words have been given to us so that we may read and recite them."
“At that time, among the assembly of Brahmās, there was a Brahmā king named Prajñādṛṣṭi who addressed the other Brahmās, saying:

‘I have now seen a Pratyekabuddha who upholds the five precepts and the eightfold fast, practices the ten wholesome deeds, and contemplates dependent origination. By means of these roots of goodness, he dedicates them toward the profound, unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment (anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi).’”
May it be that when we attain Buddhahood, our preaching of the Dharma and our deliverance of sentient beings shall exceed that of the pratyekabuddhas by hundreds of thousands of millions of times.
When I become a Buddha, may those who hear my name or behold my form swiftly eliminate immeasurable obstacles, just as I now behold this pratyekabuddha.
“When the thousand Brahmā kings had finished their offerings, they each returned to their respective abodes. After the lifespan of the Brahmā heavens had ended, they each passed away.

Following their deaths, they became a thousand wheel-turning kings over the four continents of the Sahā world, teaching through the ten wholesome paths; because of their original virtuous vows, they were not subject to [ordinary] causes and conditions, and their lifespan was eighty-four thousand years.”
"As he was about to pass away, there was a Brahmin in the Snowy Mountains who was intelligent and possessed great wisdom, with a lifespan of half a kalpa.
In a previous scripture, he had heard that in the past there was a Buddha named Candanavyūha Tathāgata, fully endowed with the ten titles."

That Buddha, the World-Honored One, preached the profound perfection of giving (dānapāramitā), wherein one does not perceive a giver nor a recipient, and practices generosity with a mind of equanimity.

At that time, having heard this matter, the Great Immortal emerged from the Snowy Mountains and went to the thousand holy kings to seek wealth and treasures, extensively praising and expounding upon the profound *dānapāramitā* for the sake of all the kings.
Lifting his right foot and raising his right hand, he stood before the king and spoke these verses:
"Generosity is a wondrous and excellent medicine; Those who take it shall never die.
One perceives neither body nor mind, And contemplates wealth and possessions as empty and still."
"The recipient is like empty space; practicing giving in this manner, with neither wealth nor recipient, is truly in accordance with the bodhisattva practice.
At that time, each of the thousand holy kings entrusted their kingdoms to their respective crown princes and issued proclamations to all the subordinate states:
"We now wish to practice all forms of giving; those who are poor and in need of wealth and treasures may come to me, and I shall bestow gifts upon them according to their wishes."
At that time, all the people of the various kingdoms gathered together at the place of the Thousand Holy Kings and addressed them, saying:
"O Holy Kings, we currently lack only two things; we require nothing else."
What are these two things?
First, celestial music;
second, celestial maidens.
At that time, the thousand holy kings took the maṇi jewels and placed them atop high banners, making this great vow:
"By our merit and the virtuous retribution we have received, which is true and not false, may these wish-fulfilling jewels cause celestial music to rain down everywhere, providing for all."
As soon as he thought this, various musical instruments rained down.
At that time, the musical instruments remained suspended in mid-air and sounded of themselves without being struck. He then formed another thought:
"If my merit and virtue are truly not in vain, may wish-fulfilling jewels rain down celestial maidens everywhere."

As soon as he thought of it, various celestial maidens rained down; their deportment was as dignified and orderly as that of the Queen of the Māras, and each celestial maiden had five hundred attendants as her retinue.
"At that time, after the Thousand Holy Kings had fulfilled the wishes of the multitude, they immediately renounced their kingdoms to leave the household life and study the Way.
Then the thousand sons of the kings, along with all the ministers and citizens, wept aloud as they followed behind the kings, escorting the Great Kings as far as the Snowy Mountains."
At that time, the Thousand Holy Kings addressed their ministers and subjects:
"All conditioned phenomena are impermanent; my body has no master; its nature and characteristics are all empty; that which exists shall return to extinction."
"I have now gained faith and understanding in this meaning; therefore, I shall renounce my kingdom without any lingering attachment.
He then followed the brahmin into the Snowy Mountains, while the prince’s ministers and subjects took their leave and returned to the country.

At that time, the thousand holy kings each established a grass hut within the Snowy Mountains; sitting upright in meditation, they gave rise to great vows to deliver all beings, seeking the unsurpassed path and contemplating the meaning of great giving.

Because of the retribution for the ten wholesome deeds performed by the Holy King in his past lives, a thousand deities from the Snowy Mountains each offered him celestial fruits, providing them daily so that he no longer sought food. Accordingly, he immediately attained the five supernormal powers, could fly through the void, and lived for one kalpa.

At that time, within the Snowy Mountains, there was a great yakṣa four thousand *li* in height, with canine fangs protruding eighty *li*, and twelve eyes on his face. From his eyes gushed blood, its radiance like molten copper; holding a sword in his left hand and a trident in his right, he stood before the noble king and cried out in a loud voice:
"I am now hungry and thirsty, having nothing to eat or drink. I only pray that the noble king, out of compassion and pity, will grant me a small portion of food."
Then the thousand holy kings said to the yakṣa:
"We make this vow: we shall give everything.
Each of them washed the yakṣa’s hands with water, gave him the fruits of the sages, and had him eat them.
The yakṣa, enraged that he had received only fruit, cast it to the ground and said to the Holy King:
"My father, a yakṣa, devours the vital essence of humans; my mother, a rākṣasī, constantly devours human hearts and drinks their warm blood.
I am now in desperate hunger and require only human hearts and blood; what use have I for fruit?"
Then, the thousand holy kings said to the yakṣa:
"Of all things that are difficult to relinquish, nothing surpasses one's own body.
We cannot today relinquish our hearts to give them to you."
At that time, the yakṣa spoke these verses:
"Observe that the mind has no marks of mind; it is composed of the four great elements and form.
To be able to relinquish all of these entirely is to accord with the conduct of a bodhisattva."
At that time, there was a brahmin in the Snowy Mountains named Raudravati, who addressed the yakṣa, saying:
"I only pray that the Great Master will preach the Dharma for me; I now do not begrudge my heart or my blood."
He immediately took off his single-layered robe, spread it out to serve as a high seat, and invited the yakṣa to take this seat.
At that time, the Great Yakṣa spoke in verse:
“Desiring to seek the path of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), One does not begrudge even a portion of one’s body or mind.”
Though subjected to the many sufferings of mutilation, one endures them as the earth does;
nor does one perceive a self who receives them. Seeking the Dharma with a heart free of regret, one has no stinginess toward anything at all, like one whose head is on fire.
"To universally relieve the hunger and thirst of all beings—this is what accords with the conduct of a Bodhisattva.
When Lohitaka heard this verse, his body and mind were filled with joy; he immediately took a sharp sword, pierced his chest, and drew out his heart.
At that time, an earth deity emerged from the ground and said to Lohitākṣa:
"I pray only that you, Great Seer, will have compassion for us and for the deities of the mountains and trees; do not sacrifice your life for the sake of a single ghost."
Then, Rādha addressed the deities, saying:
"This body is like a phantom or a mirage; As soon as it appears, it changes and perishes.
It is like the sound of an echo; Once called, it no longer responds."
The power of the four elements and five aggregates—its momentum will not endure for long.
Throughout millions of billions of years, I have never died for the sake of the Dharma;
now, for the sake of the Dharma, I offer my heart’s blood as a gift.
Be careful not to stubbornly obstruct me, hindering my unsurpassed wisdom.
In recompense for this act of giving, I vow to attain the Way of the Buddha;
when I later achieve Buddhahood, I shall first deliver you all.
Having spoken this verse, he lay down before the yakṣa and pierced his own neck with a sword to give his blood to the yakṣa; he then further tore open his chest and gave him his heart.
"At that time, heaven and earth shook violently; the sun lost its brilliance, and thunder resounded though there were no clouds.
Five yakṣas came from the four directions, vying with one another to tear him apart and contending to devour him."
Having finished eating, he let out a great cry and leaped into the air, addressing the thousand holy kings:
"Who among you can practice giving as Rādha did?
Only by practicing such giving can one attain Buddhahood."
At that time, the thousand holy kings were struck with terror and despondency; they no longer desired awakening, but gave rise to regretful thoughts and each wished to return to their own kingdoms.
Then, the five yakṣas spoke these verses:
"Non-killing is the seed of the Buddha; A compassionate heart is the supreme medicine."
Great Compassion is ever peaceful and secure, never subject to the changes of aging or death.
All who possess a body fear those who kill and harm them;
for this reason, the Bodhisattvas teach the practice of the precept against killing.
If you now fear death, you ought to practice non-killing;
why do you wish to return to your kingdom,
abandoning tranquility for the clamor of the world?
When the thousand holy kings heard these words, they all remained silent.
The Buddha told Bhadrapāla:
“You should now know that the first brāhmaṇa, who praised the perfection of giving (dānapāramitā), was the Tathāgata King of Fixed Radiance (Niyataprakāśarāja) in the past.”
Rādha was, in the past, the Buddha Dīpaṃkara.

At that time, when a thousand holy kings left the household life to study the Path, they saw Dīpaṃkara Buddha practicing various ascetic austerities; their hearts were filled with regret and remorse, and for one kalpa they fell into the great hells.
Although they fell into hell, because their minds were adorned by the power of their vow for bodhi, the fires could not burn them.

From that time forward, he again encountered the Bodhisattva King of Lamp-Light, who preached the Dharma for him. Emerging from the hells, he extensively praised the thousand Buddhas of the past—beginning with the Buddha Adornment of Liberation and Renown, and ending with the final Buddha, King of Sublime Sovereignty.

At that time, the thousand holy kings heard the names of the thousand Buddhas; filled with joy, they paid them homage. By this cause and condition, they transcended the offenses of birth and death for nine hundred million nayutas of Ganges-sands of kalpas.
Bhadrapāla! You should know now: were those thousand holy kings anyone else?
They are none other than we, the thousand Buddhas of this Bhadrakalpa.
When the Buddha had spoken these words, the entire great assembly, having heard what the Buddha taught, were all filled with great joy.
Eighty people resolved their minds upon the unsurpassed path;
two hundred and fifty people, their outflows exhausted and their minds liberated, became arhats.
"Furthermore, Bhadrapāla!
In the past, immeasurable, incalculable, and countless asaṃkhyeya kalpas ago, there was a great king in this Jambudvīpa named Sujāti, and his kingdom was called Vijayadhvaja."

When that king was born, the seven treasures supported his feet, and thirty-four auspicious omens descended from heaven. As soon as he touched the ground, he began to walk, and the seven treasures arrived spontaneously. From the mountains in the four directions, one hundred million immortals and seers, fully endowed with the five supernatural powers, flew together to assemble before the palace.

Furthermore, hundreds of thousands of millions of *Ganges*-sands of great mountains made of the seven treasures surged forth and stood in the air before the palace, corresponding to the presence of the immortals and seers.
King Śūradatta gradually grew up and ruled over the four continents; his majesty and virtue were sovereign, and he transformed the people through the ten wholesome paths of action.
By the power of the King’s virtue, all the subjects experienced happiness just like that of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven.

At that time, the various seers each took up a seer-scripture and presented it to the king, instructing him to read it. Having finished reading the scripture, the king heard that in the past there was a Buddha named Ratnakusuma-vaidūrya-guṇaprabhāsa-śrī-tathāgata, who was fully endowed with the ten titles.
Upon hearing the name of the Buddha, the king’s body and mind were filled with joy; he immediately removed his jeweled crown, prostrated toward the four directions, and made this great vow:
"Today I renounce all that is precious within the four continents and leave the home life to study the Way, sitting beneath the Bodhi tree of Radiance with body and mind unmoving."
"If I do not attain Anuttara-samyak-sambodhi, I shall never rise from here.

At that time, the King of the Six Heavens of Desire, named Vajra-maṇi-ratna, together with eighty trillion demons and their ghostly armies—each manifesting ten billion terrifying transformations—vied with one another to assemble at the Bodhi tree.

At that time, King Śūradatta sat upright beneath a tree and entered the Samādhi of the King of Compassionate Mind Sealed by Wisdom; by the power of this samādhi, the hosts of Māra’s armies were simultaneously shattered and destroyed. After seventy-seven days had passed, he attained Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
"At that time, all the celestial seers came together to entreat him to turn the sublime Wheel of Dharma.
Among the assembly of seers was a great seer named Prabhāphala, who spoke a verse of entreaty, saying:
'Virtuous One, Viśvantara, You are a Golden-Wheel King of the four realms.'"
Now he has renounced these seven treasures, as a bird sheds a single feather.
Seated beneath the tree of radiance, he has subdued ten trillion māras;
having heard the Dharma of ambrosia, his cultivation of the Path is perfected.
With marks and signs peerless and extraordinary, His majestic light illuminates the ten directions;
He shall be named Great Sage of Perfect Tranquility— We pray that he will surely deliver us.
Now, with our heads bowed in prostration, we pay homage And entreat him to turn the Wheel of Dharma.
"The second seer, named Prabhāsaṃcaya, further spoke in verse:
'The Great Sage, out of compassion for sentient beings, Vowed to sit beneath the tree;
Having subdued all the hosts of Māra, The ocean of fetters has been exhausted. "
"Out of compassion for all sentient beings, please extensively expound the Dharma of the Deathless.

At that time, the World-Honored One silently accepted the request of the rishis and, beneath the Bodhi tree of Radiance, turned the wondrous Wheel of Dharma. He emitted light from his entire body that illuminated the worlds of the ten directions, making them all golden in color. He extensively expounded upon the Four Noble Truths and the Twelve Links of Dependent Origination in a total of ten billion verses.

In the first assembly, the seers from the four mountains who heard the Dharma all attained the patience of the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*); hundreds of thousands of people resolved their minds on the unsurpassed path and left home to study the Way; countless members of the fourfold assembly attained the stage of *srotāpanna*, and those who resolved their minds on *bodhicitta* were beyond calculation.

The lifespan of that Buddha was two hundred and fifty thousand kalpas; the True Dharma remained in the world for two million kalpas, and the Semblance Dharma remained in the world for four million kalpas.
When the Dharma of that World-Honored Buddha was about to perish, there were bhikṣus who traveled about to teach and transform others.
At that time, there was a country named Vidyutprabha, where there lived an elder named Rādha who practiced the ways of non-Buddhist paths and served the Dharma of Brahmā.
King Dīptārcis dispatched a thousand youths to provide for that man by sweeping and cleaning the celestial temple.
At that time, as each of the thousand youths was carrying celestial flowers intending to go to the temple, they saw on the road various bhikṣus walking with images of the Buddha. The youths asked:
"What deity is this, so upright and majestic, whose splendor is so sublime?"
The bhikṣus said, "This is the image of Mahāpraśānta. The youth asked:
"O Great Well-Quiescent One!
From what lineage are you born?
What is your meaning?"
The bhikṣu replied: "Do you not know?

Long ago in the distant past, King Sujāti abandoned his kingdom to leave the household life and attain the unsurpassed path, being titled the Great Sublime Tranquility (Mahāśānti). He entered parinirvāṇa in the Forest of Pure Light."
"We are now his disciples; what we hold is the image of the Sublime Peace.
At that time, having heard the Buddha’s account of the causes and conditions, the thousand youths each took a lotus flower to offer to the image and prostrated at its feet.

“Bhadrapāla! You should now know that by virtue of these causes and conditions of making offerings to the Buddha’s image, those boys, according to the length of their respective lifespans, will each pass away; after passing away, they will immediately encounter sixty billion nayutas of Buddhas, attend upon and make offerings to them, and attain non-retrogression from the unsurpassed path.”
Bhadrapāla! You should now know that among those sages of the four mountains in the world of that Buddha, whose number is beyond reckoning, have each now attained Buddhahood in the ten directions.
As for those thousand youths who made offerings of flowers at that time, could they have been anyone else?
They are none other than we, the thousand Buddhas of the Bhadrakalpa, Bhadrapāla!

You should now know that after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, if any of the fourfold assembly should offer even a single flower as an offering to a Buddha image, they will obtain two kinds of merit. What are these two?
First, they always attain birth by transformation;
second, their physical form is upright and handsome.
Furthermore, they obtain two fruits:
"First, they will always encounter the Buddhas;
second, they will be born many times in the heavens.
When the bhikṣus heard what the Buddha had said, they all rejoiced greatly.
The Buddha told Bhadrapāla:

“You should now know that I recall, from immeasurable, countless, thousands of myriads of koṭis of kalpas in the past, there was a Buddha named Ratnacchatrābhyudgatarāja Tathāgata, Arhat, fully endowed with the ten titles.”
"When that Buddha appears in the world, this trichiliocosm will be equal to the Vajra Buddha-field, without any difference.
The Tathāgata Jewel Canopy Illuminating Space also teaches and transforms sentient beings by means of the three vehicles."

After the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, during the period of the Semblance Dharma, there was an elder named Candrasamudgata who traveled through villages to teach and transform sentient beings. He praised the name of the Tathāgata Ratnacchatrābhyudgatarāja with these verses:
“The Tathāgata Ratnacchatrābhyudgatarāja, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, The unsurpassed Tamer, Teacher of Gods and Men;
The Lion of the Śākyas, long free from birth and death, Possessing untainted, pure, and authentic wisdom.”
Capable of serving as a sublime field of merit for the world, universally saving all like a king of physicians;
hearing whose name one surely attains great liberation—I now prostrate to the Unsurpassed Victor.
When the elder had spoken these verses, he made offerings of various flowers and incense to the image of the Buddha, "Jewel Canopy Illuminating the Void.

Having completed the floral offerings, a thousand bhikṣus entered the lecture hall; seeing the great elder making offerings of flowers and incense and reciting verses of praise for the Buddha, they were moved.
The first bhikṣu, named Sūryagarbha, asked the elder:
"What do you seek by making offerings of daily incense and flowers and praising the name of the Buddha today?"
The householder said:
"Venerable Bhikṣu! You should listen with a single-minded focus."
"Now I make this offering because I wish to seek the unsurpassed, equal Great Way.
The bhikṣu asked: "What is meant by the 'unsurpassed Great Way'?"
The elder replied: "Without attachment and without dependence, free from burdens with a tranquil mind,
one's original nature is like space— this is called the Unsurpassed Way."
The conduct of the Great Man has compassion as its supreme quality;
adorned with the thirty-seven factors that extinguish the mind and the power of awakening,
he boards the ship of the six perfections to forever cross the stream of birth and death.
In that state, the mind is without attachment; therefore, it is called the Unsurpassed Way.
The Buddha’s wisdom is like Mount Sumeru, and also like a blooming lotus flower;
having long since realized the nature of emptiness, it is therefore called the Unsurpassed Way.
The Tamer knows that the mind is suchness; the nature of the limit of reality is likewise so.
All that exists within the three realms enters into the quiescence of suchness;
being untamed, they possess the mark of non-arising, and thus equally enter the nature of the Dharma-realm.
"Since there is thus nothing that exists, it is called the Unsurpassed Way.
When the elder had spoken this verse, he addressed the bhikṣu, saying:
"I only pray that the Great Virtuous One will practice the Unsurpassed Way!"
The Bhikṣu Sūryagarbha spoke again in verse:
"According to the meaning you have explained, there is no practice and nothing to rely upon;
the nature and characteristics of all things are empty and quiescent— what dharma should I then practice?"
I have asked about the Great Way, desiring to know the Buddha’s awakened wisdom;
now you speak of the characteristics of the dharma-realm, which is as unknowable as empty space.
Within this unknowability, there is no desire and nothing to be sought.
"When such natures and characteristics have ceased, what should I do?
At that time, the elder spoke again in verse:
"The sun’s rays abide in the sky, universally illuminating all things."
That [light] likewise has no mental characteristics; it desires to shatter all darkness and gloom.
With the power of its radiance shining forth, it transcends all obscurity.
Both darkness and light are entirely devoid of mind or intention.
The fundamental nature is non-abiding darkness; the nature of darkness does not pause for even a moment.
The Buddha’s wisdom is likewise: neither extinguished nor produced.
Adorned with the path of the power of knowledge, it arises from the five eyes.
The six supernormal powers are like lotus flowers, unstained by and unattached to the world.
Adorned with morality, concentration, and wisdom, they transcend all worldly appearances;
therefore, one should take refuge in this unsurpassed, equal path.
At that time, having spoken this verse, the elder addressed the bhikṣu, saying:
"Virtuous One!
Do you now wish to seek the unsurpassed path?"
Upon hearing the words of the elder, the bhikṣu Sūryagarbha deeply understood their meaning and purpose. He prostrated at the Buddha’s feet and spoke these verses:

“I prostrate at the feet of the Buddha, the Great Liberation, Who dwells long in nirvāṇa, extinguishing all modes of existence, Adorned with the power of untainted wisdom— Just as the elder has described this wisdom of quiescence.”
I now seek to be free from defilement and entanglement, transcending all empty marks of the world;
I now seek the path of quiescent extinction, neither bound nor liberated, and not abiding in form.
Furthermore, I do not enter into the midst of bondage or liberation; there is no mark of birth-and-death or of emancipation.
This place is called the Path of Ambrosia; may I attain the fruition as I have vowed.

By practicing the six perfections without hindrance or burden, I shall certainly abide in the Śūraṅgama Samādhi, possessing the rank, dignity, and conduct of a Buddha, and fulfilling Buddha-wisdom like the Buddhas of the past.
The indestructible diamond nature of emptiness-wisdom, The activity of the Great Person of All-Knowledge,
The wish-fulfilling king of maṇi jewels— I too shall attain this mark of oneness,
The supreme nature of the impartial mind of deliverance.
At that time, having spoken these verses, the bhikṣu addressed the householder, saying:
"You should now know that I have understood the meaning of the verses you spoke; I am now a fit vessel for bodhi."

"We, the thousand bhikṣus, from this day forth until we attain Buddhahood, shall constantly cultivate great compassion and love all universally; we shall not give rise to disparagement toward any sentient beings, much less kill them."

“From this day forth until I attain enlightenment, I shall constantly give rise to great compassion to universally embrace all beings; yet within that great compassion, I shall not give rise to the perception of compassion, nor shall I produce any attachment.”

“From this day forth until I attain Buddhahood, when I see others obtain happiness, my mind shall give rise to joy, just as a bhikṣu attains the bliss of the third dhyāna, yet without giving rise to the touch of pleasure or the perception of pleasure.”
“From this day forth until I attain Buddhahood, I shall not perceive sentient beings nor the mark of sentient beings; furthermore, I shall neither dwell in joy nor enter into equanimity.”
“From this day forth until I attain Buddhahood, I shall never engage in any of the ninety-five kinds of evil, unrighteous observances.
From this day forth until I attain Buddhahood, I shall never, for my own sake, keep the eight kinds of impure things;
if I should accumulate anything, it shall be solely for the benefit of all sentient beings.”
“From this day forth until I attain Buddhahood, I shall never slander the Dharma-treasury of the Bodhisattvas;

even if there were one with eloquence and boundless wisdom who preached a doctrine of false views for a full hundred thousand years, I would rather have my body shattered into atoms than ever believe or accept it.”

“From this day forth until I attain Buddhahood, should there be sentient beings who do not cultivate wholesome karma but instead commit the five heinous crimes, I shall certainly teach and transform them so that they may obtain benefit.”
“From this day forth until I attain Buddhahood, I vow to deliver all sentient beings submerged in suffering within the five turbidities of this evil world.
From this day forth until I attain Buddhahood, I shall constantly practice the various pāramitās, reaching their ultimate limit to arrive at the shore of Great Wisdom.”
“From this day forth until I attain Buddhahood, I shall never abandon any sentient being, but shall surely comfort them and benefit them with the Dharma.

From this day forth until I attain Buddhahood, I vow to universally adorn all Buddha-works, cultivate all pure practices, take the ten kinds of precious jewels as my feet, and take the liberation of wishlessness as my eyes, so that I may roam in the great void of ultimate nirvana.”
At that time, after the thousand bhikṣus had made this vow, they prostrated themselves with their five limbs touching the ground to pay homage to all the Buddhas, and spoke these verses:
“The Buddha’s wisdom is unshakable, Born from liberation;
Its fundamental nature and characteristics are inherently empty, It is the playful sport of the vajra-mind.”
“Having already crushed the demon of afflictions, with the aggregates and hindrances forever eliminated,
I now prostrate my head before the one of pure great wisdom.
Having spoken this verse, he paid homage to all Buddhas throughout the ten directions.
At that time, thunder resounded in a cloudless sky, and the devas, nāgas, and spirits rained down celestial flowers as an offering, uttering these verses:
“Excellent, O Supreme Great Being!
Living by begging for sustenance, he always remained free from the four kinds of food;
clad in dyed robes and holding an alms-bowl, his great number reached a full thousand.
Now, once again, he has given rise to the most supreme and subtle mind of enlightenment.
"The field of merit most supreme, None surpasses the community of bhikṣus;
I now prostrate with my head at their feet— To those who practice the Mahāyāna.

At that time, having heard this verse praising their virtues, the thousand bhikṣus redoubled their diligence and immediately attained the profound Samādhi of Contemplating the Buddha. They then addressed the elder, saying:
"Excellent, householder!
It is because of you that I have resolved to attain bodhicitta; you, too, should leave the household life to study the Way within the ocean of the Buddha-dharma."

At that time, the elder accepted the bhikṣu’s instruction, left the household life to study the Path within the True Dharma, constantly practiced the dhūta austerities, and performed all manner of ascetic disciplines; after seventy-seven days had passed, he attained the patience of the non-arising of phenomena (anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti).

"Bhadrapāla! You should know now that the great elder who at that time taught and inspired many people to resolve upon bodhicitta has long since attained buddhahood; he is the Buddha Viśeṣacandrarāja."

If there are good men or good women who hear these names of the Buddhas, they will always encounter the Buddhas and attain non-retrogression in their resolve for Bodhicitta; they shall immediately transcend the most grievous evil karma of twelve hundred million kalpas.
"The thousand bhikṣus who then made this vow are none other than us, the thousand Buddhas of the Bhadrakalpa.

When these words were spoken, a hundred thousand Brahmā kings resolved their minds upon Bodhicitta; one thousand upāsakas and others attained the realization of the non-arising of dharmas (anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti); and five hundred bhikṣuṇīs, including the mother of Uttara and the bhikṣuṇī Bhadrikā, with minds free from all outflows (anāsrava), attained liberation and became arhats.
When these words were spoken, the great assembly gathered at that time, having heard what the Buddha had said, all rejoiced greatly.
The Buddha addressed Bhadrapāla:
"You should now know that I recall, in the past, immeasurable, countless, asaṃkhyeya kalpas ago, there was a Buddha named Śuddhasvara Tathāgata, fully endowed with the ten titles."
When that Buddha appeared in the world, this trichiliocosm was adorned with the seven treasures, being no different from the Land of Jewel Adornment.

The Buddha’s lifespan was twenty great kalpas; the True Dharma remained in the world for forty kalpas, and the Semblance Dharma remained for twice as long, eighty kalpas, likewise teaching and transforming sentient beings through the three vehicles.

“In the period of the Semblance Dharma, there will be a bhikṣu named Sarvakṣānti, who upholds the Bodhisattva-piṭaka and practices the Bodhisattva-dharma. Traveling through villages, he will constantly recite this verse:
“The Buddha abides in equanimous emptiness; The nature and characteristics of the Dharma are likewise so.
The Saṃgha relies upon the unconditioned assembly; The meaning of the Three Jewels is without distinction.”
"Having realized that the fundamental nature of all things is empty, Taking refuge in the state of quiescent extinction,
And constantly practicing the path of True Suchness— This is what accords with the conduct of a Bodhisattva.
The Great Bhikṣu Kṣāntivādī (Patience-Preacher) constantly recited this verse.

At that time, there were a thousand brahmins in the Flower-Light Forest who practiced the four Brahma-vihāras—loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity. Upon hearing this bhikṣu praise the meaning of the names of the Triple Gem, their bodies and minds were filled with joy, and they immediately addressed the bhikṣu:
"In which sūtra is there such a meaning?"
The bhikṣu said: “Great Tamer!
In the Great Vaipulya Sūtra of Reality, it is taught that the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṃgha are equal in the wisdom of emptiness, abiding within the single characteristic.”

“At that time, the thousand brahmins, having heard of the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Sangha’s wisdom of the equality of emptiness, immediately contemplated the meaning of the profound and great wisdom of emptiness.

For eight thousand years they sat upright in meditative absorption (*samādhi*), yet within the dharma of emptiness they did not reach full realization. They further contemplated the emptiness of all dharmas, yet even regarding the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*) they did not reach full realization; nevertheless, they gave rise to neither doubt nor slander, maintaining this contemplation.”
At that time, there was a bhikṣu named Jñānagarbha who addressed the brahmins:

"Do you know? In the past, there was a Buddha named Samādhirāja-Abhyudgata Tathāgata, fully endowed with the ten titles; likewise, hundreds of thousands of billions of Buddhas with these same names all preached the profound Prajñāpāramitā."
That sutra states:
"Do not dwell in any phenomena; the nature of all phenomena is empty.
Thus, O Brahmin, if your mind is not clear regarding these empty phenomena, you should simply focus your mind single-pointedly on the meaning of emptiness.
When the thousand brahmins heard these words, their hearts were filled with great joy, and they said to the bhikṣu:

“The Prajñāpāramitā is the wisdom of great emptiness. We are currently shrouded by ignorance and have no means to comprehend the meaning of emptiness; we can only rejoice in body and mind within the Dharma taught by your venerable self.”
The Buddha told Bhadrapāla:
"As for those two bhikṣus who were skilled in preaching the Dharma, the first bhikṣu has now attained Buddhahood in the Land of Wondrous Joy as the Buddha Joyful Adornment Jewel King.

If any of the fourfold assembly hears the name of that Buddha, prostrates themselves with their five limbs touching the ground, and takes refuge and pays homage, they shall immediately transcend the sins of birth and death for five hundred trillion asaṃkhyeya kalpas."
The second bhikṣu has long since attained Buddhahood, being named Tathāgata Imperial Jewel Banner Maṇi Supreme Radiance, fully endowed with the ten titles;

if any of the fourfold assembly hears that Buddha’s name, prostrates themselves on the ground with their five limbs, and takes refuge and pays homage, they shall immediately transcend the sins of birth and death for seven hundred trillion asaṃkhyeya kalpas.

At that time, the thousand brahmins, having heard this profound *prajñāpāramitā*, were filled with joy in body and mind; they gave rise to no alarm, doubt, fear, or slander, and immediately transcended the offenses of birth and death for fifty billion kalpas.

After relinquishing his body in this world, he immediately encountered sixteen hundred million buddhas and attained the *buddhānusmṛti-samādhi* (the samādhi of mindfulness of the Buddha) under those buddhas.
Because his mind was adorned by the *buddhānusmṛti-samādhi*, through the adornment of that samādhi, his mind gradually attained realization and liberation regarding the dharma of emptiness.
"Bhadrapāla! As for those thousand brahmins at that time, were they anyone else?

They are none other than us, the thousand Buddhas of the Bhadrakalpa. Because we heard the Dharma of emptiness and our minds were free from doubt, we have successively attained *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* in this Sahā world."
"Therefore, all sentient beings should have no doubt or uncertainty in their minds regarding the meaning of emptiness.

When the Buddha spoke these words, the great assembly present heard what the Buddha had said; some attained the first fruit [of the path], and some resolved to attain the unsurpassed, right, and true Way, their number being so vast that it cannot be fully recounted.
When the entire great assembly heard what the Buddha had spoken, they were all filled with great joy and prostrated at the Buddha’s feet.
The Buddha addressed Bhadrapāla:

“I recall that in the past, immeasurable, innumerable, and incalculable *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas ago, there was a Buddha in that world named Sāgarabuddhi Tathāgata, who was fully endowed with the ten titles.”
The land is named Pure Joy; adorned with the seven treasures, the ground produces precious flowers, like Mount Sumeru composed of the seven treasures, magnificent, radiant, and lovely.

That Buddha, the World-Honored One, constantly enters meditative concentration and remains silent without speaking, never preaching the Dharma; he performs the work of a Buddha solely by emitting the light from the mark of the great man between his eyebrows.
There are some sentient beings who, seeing the light of the white tuft like the seal of the ten wholesome actions, hear it explain the meaning of the ten wholesome actions;
some see the light of the white tuft like the seal of the five precepts, hearing it explain the meaning of the five precepts and the conditions for the five precepts;
and some see the light of the white tuft like the seal of the eight precepts, hearing it explain the meaning of the eight precepts and the conditions for the eight precepts.
There are some sentient beings who see the light of the white tuft as the seal of the *Prātimokṣa*, whereby it explains the meaning of the *Prātimokṣa* and the conditions for the *Prātimokṣa*;
there are some sentient beings who see the light of the white tuft as the seal of the six *pāramitās*, whereby it explains the meaning of the eighty-four thousand perfections;

and there are some sentient beings who see the light of the white tuft as the seal of the four truths, whereby it explains the meaning of the four truths and the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment.
There may be sentient beings who, seeing the light of the white tuft like the seal of a Pratyekabuddha, explain the meaning of the twelve links of dependent origination;

or there may be sentient beings who, seeing the light of the white tuft like the seal of the mark of wisdom, expound upon the realms of the Bodhisattva from the first stage up to the tenth stage, speak of the Samādhi of the Seal of Light of Śūraṅgama, and speak of the indestructible realm of the Vajra-samādhi.

"Bhadrapāla! Within this mark of the great man, the white tuft of hair between the brows, there appear immeasurable and innumerable seals as numerous as the sands of the Ganges. In some seals, the fearless proclamation of the Dharma is performed;
in others, the ninety-five kinds of heterodox and erroneous arts of the non-Buddhists are expounded."
In some mudrās, the sublime karmic retributions of the various celestial hosts are explained;
in some mudrās, the formation and destruction of kalpas are explained;
and in some mudrās, the sun, moon, five planets, twenty-eight lunar mansions, as well as all worldly affairs such as calamities, anomalies, and strange portents, are explained.
Furthermore, among the mudrās, there are those that speak of the paths of the various ṛṣis and spirits:

"This white-hair (ūrṇā) mudrā universally illuminates the ten directions to transform and deliver sentient beings, manifesting buddha-activities according to those with whom there is a karmic affinity."
That Buddha’s lifespan was twelve great kalpas; the True Dharma remained in the world for another twelve kalpas, and the Semblance Dharma remained for twenty-four kalpas.
During the period of the Semblance Dharma, there were one thousand brahmins; the first brahmin was named Dānaśreṣṭha, and the last was named Bhadraśreṣṭha.
There were one thousand brahmins, all of whom were intelligent and possessed vast knowledge, each thoroughly versed in the four Vedas.
During the period of the Semblance Dharma of the Tathāgata Sāgarabuddhi, there was a bhikṣu named Viśuddhanāga-Abhirūpa-alaṃkāra, who engaged in debate and refutation with these brahmins.

The Brahmins expounded the Vedic scriptures and the doctrines of the *puruṣa*, while the śramaṇas, in turn, proclaimed the profound meaning of emptiness through the twelve divisions of the sūtras, teaching the signless to destroy their attachments.
When the thousand brahmins heard the meaning of signlessness, they said to the bhikṣu,
“From where did you obtain this Dharma of selflessness, emptiness,
and quiescence? The bhikṣu replied:
"The Buddhas of the three periods of time, fully endowed with the ten titles, have all together proclaimed this.
Within the mark of the white tuft between the eyebrows of the Tathāgata Sāgarabuddhi, he constantly recites this verse:
'The meaning of the original nature is non-arising; There is neither recipient nor taker. "
The nature of the four great elements is like an illusion; the five aggregates are like a mirage or lightning.
All worlds in existence are like a whirling firebrand, all turning in accordance with ignorance and arising through the adornment of the power of karma.
Contemplate that nature and characteristics are impermanent, Without self and without arising;
the wise should carefully observe The meaning of causes and conditions from beginning to end.
The fundamental nature and the limit of reality are empty, Yet through attachment, one falsely perceives them as existent.
If one can thoroughly understand emptiness, The sphere of wishlessness and non-action,
Signless and without dependence, One will surely attain the Way like the Buddha,
Subduing all demonic adversaries And delivering all devas and humans.
"Furthermore, one enters the Great Liberation; Knowing that emptiness is the fundamental retribution— This is what the Buddha has taught: The meaning of non-self and emptiness.

Having spoken this verse, the thousand brahmins were filled with great joy in their hearts. They prostrated at the feet of the bhikṣu and each returned to their respective homes. Seated upright in the forest wilds, they contemplated non-self and emptiness.

After eight million years, his mind remained undecided regarding the meaning of the Great Emptiness (*mahā-śūnyatā*). By the power of the merit from contemplating the meaning of emptiness, he immediately beheld hundreds of thousands of Buddhas within space. Having attained the Buddha-remembrance samādhi (*buddhānusmṛti-samādhi*) in the presence of those Buddhas, he saw within the mark of the ūrṇā-kośa of the Buddha Sāgarabuddhi the recitation of these verses of nectar:
"If you wish to give rise to the bodhicitta, And practice and uphold the Bodhisattva precepts, If you seek true emptiness, Follow and study the path of the Bodhisattvas."
One should always practice a mind of loving-kindness, Eliminating thoughts of anger and harm;
With compassion for all beings, One contemplates their bodies as empty and quiescent.
My own body has no inherent nature or characteristics; It arises dependently upon the four great elements.
In accordance with the teachings of all Buddhas, They do not kill and give rise to no anger.
Fully capable of receiving all dharmas, Their minds are like the earth;
Always acting without attachment, With single-minded focus they abide in one-pointedness.
"Observe that all phenomena are equal; There is neither 'that' nor 'this.
Contemplate this meaning with a correct mind, And you shall accord with the conduct of a bodhisattva.

At that time, having heard these verses, the thousand brahmins were filled with joy in body and mind. They redoubled their diligence and immediately attained the Samādhi of the Manifest Presence of All Buddhas. Within that samādhi, they entered into firm and correct meditative absorption (*samāpatti*), never again regressing from the mind set upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
"Bhadrapāla! At that time, the bhikṣu Vyūharāja, who was so abundant in nāgas, has long since attained Buddhahood; he is the Buddha Nāgeśvararāja in the land of Padmaprabha.
As for those thousand brahmins, could they possibly be anyone else?"
"We are the thousand Buddhas of this Bhadrakalpa. Bhadrapāla!

I and the thousand Buddhas of the Bhadrakalpa, while within the bequeathed Dharma of the Tathāgata Sāgaramatī, heard these verses on Great Emptiness; though we sat in contemplation with minds that did not yet fully comprehend them, we were nevertheless able to transcend the offenses of birth and death for immeasurable billions of kalpas."
"Therefore, you all should contemplate and realize the meaning of emptiness.

At that time, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, some in the assembly attained the first fruit [of the path], some resolved upon the unsurpassed, right, and true path, and some planted the causes and conditions for the path of a pratyekabuddha.
When the great assembly heard what the Buddha had said, they were all filled with immense joy. "Bhadrapāla!
I recall that in the past, immeasurable billions of eons ago, there was a Buddha named Svayambhūjaya Tathāgata, who was fully endowed with the ten titles."
When that Buddha, the World-Honored One, appeared in the world, the ground of this Sahā world became golden in color, and golden flowers and golden light filled the world.

The lifespan of the Tathāgata Svairavijaya was fifty great kalpas; the True Dharma remained in the world for thirty great kalpas, and the Semblance Dharma remained in the world for one hundred and twenty great kalpas.

During the period of the Semblance Dharma, there were a thousand lay devotees who possessed abundant wealth and treasures, each storing one hundred million; yet, although they obtained worldly profit, they did not rejoice in it, but constantly cultivated the perceptions of suffering, emptiness, and impermanence.
At that time, there was in the world an upāsaka named Mahānāga, who was intelligent and possessed great wisdom. He went to the householder’s place and spoke these verses in a loud voice:
“Wealth is a thing without an owner; It is plundered by kings and thieves.
Exhausted by water, fire, and wind, It brings no peace and does not endure.”
This body belongs to impermanence, Constantly driven by old age and illness;
Hurriedly attending to myriad affairs, One fails to perceive the suffering of the thief of death.
Dissolved by the force of the wind of impermanence, Wealth is like a great venomous serpent.
Poison is more fierce than dragons, and it is likewise a universal enemy.
The Buddhas and the noble sages regard wealth as a festering sore;
they cast it away upon the great earth, just as a person discards mucus and spittle.
When a virtuous person practices generosity, they constantly contemplate non-self;
that the wealth, the recipient, and the three factors involved are all empty and quiescent—
adorned with this, one truly accords with the conduct of a Bodhisattva.

At that time, the thousand householders, having heard the meaning of the verses spoken by the upāsaka, were filled with profound joy at such an unprecedented experience; they immediately followed him together to the monastic quarters.
Having arrived at the monks' quarters, he addressed the bhikṣus:
"In this great assembly, who possesses wisdom?
I only pray that you will preach the Dharma of the Deathless for me!"
At that time, there was a bhikṣu in the assembly named Viśuddhasvara, who extensively praised the bodhisattva’s dānapāramitā to the lay devotees, and spoke these verses:
“In the past there was a Buddha, Named Svayambhūjaya; That World-Honored One Constantly preached this Dharma.”
Generosity forms a sublime accumulation; its retribution is inexhaustible. Devas and worldlings alike are established by means of giving.
One should practice and cultivate generosity; generosity is like a precious canopy that shelters the destitute.
In this life and the next, one will dwell in peace and happiness wherever one is born.
Cultivating the mind of the wisdom of emptiness, one does not abide in any form of existence while practicing giving;
such a giver will surely attain the Way of the Buddha.
"The Dharma of giving (*dāna*) taught by the Buddhas of antiquity—householder, you should keep this in mind and practice it at the proper time.
At that time, the thousand householders, hearing again the bhikṣu’s praise of giving, felt joy in both body and mind.
They immediately went to the king's presence and addressed him, saying:
"Today we have heard the bhikṣus praising and expounding upon the dānapāramitā.
We only pray that Your Majesty will proclaim it for us, so that all the impoverished and suffering beings within the kingdom may universally hear and know of it!"
The Sutra on the Causes and Conditions of the Thousand Buddhas Spoken by the Buddha.
